Even hormone treatments and calcium replacement therapies don’t address all of the physical concerns, as Belters have a tendency to be slender and less-muscled than Earthers or Martians, with obvious physical signs such as spine ridges where the bones didn’t fuse properly. These Belters suffer from a number of physical ailments and can’t tolerate Earth’s gravity outside large, liquid-filled buoyancy

“Aggression against the Belt is what Earth and Mars survive on. Our weakness is their strength,” the masked woman said from Miller’s terminal screen. The split circle of the OPA draped behind her, like something painted on a sheet. “Don’t be afraid of them. Their only power is your fear.” “Well, that and a hundred or so gunships,” Havelock said.

— Leviathan Wakes

THE TRANSPORT UNION tanks—being forced into a gravity well outside these tanks is torture for them, both legally and literally. Besides the physical ailments caused by microgravity, some Belters suffer brain damage caused by hypoxia—the result of improperly-cleaned air filters or low oxygen levels. Other Belters suffer from malnutrition, as nearly all food must be imported from Earth, Mars, or the “Belter breadbasket” greenhouses on Europa and Ganymede. Dehydration is also a constant concern, as all water in the Belt is either heavily recycled or comes from ice brought in by haulers from the rest of the Belt or the rings of Saturn. Mining is dangerous work no matter what’s being mined—a disproportionately large number of Belters replace damaged or destroyed limbs with prosthetics, a more affordable option despite the ability to regrow missing limbs being widely available, at least on the inner planets.

Belter Life

Most Belters live in small apartments called “holes,” which are often literal holes bored into the rock of asteroids. The nicer areas are lit by recessed lights, with green floors and blue ceilings to trick the body into thinking of Earth. The trickery is aided by pseudo scents to drown out the antiseptic smell of sealant and recycled air and water. Vast neighborhoods are separated by corridors, linked by air filtration systems and massive metal ducts that collect fungi and detritus unless they’re constantly scrubbed clean. The close living quarters lend to the odd combination of civic pride and self-reliance. Belters walk from corridor to corridor, take public transport tubes, and live their lives within close reach of their neighbors. No asteroid is naturally fit for human life, nor can they be terraformed like Mars. Nothing will grow in solid rock, and no air clings to a dwarf planet. Every breath a Belter takes comes through an air filter, and every breath is shared with a thousand others. Keeping filters clean, water purifiers humming, and fungus tanks properly shielded are tasks for the entire community. When the authorities are shipped in from corporations on Luna or Earth, they can’t be trusted. Belters look out for each other as a matter of course, and when a Belter fails in their duties or commits an offense, it’s dealt with as a community matter. When something breaks, it gets fixed—or at least it gets pointed out to someone who can fix it. Problems or maintenance that go unaddressed in space tend to result in people dying.

Relations With the Inners

There’s a truism in the Belt: Belters are needed, but not wanted. Especially true prior to the opening of the Ring gates, Earth and Mars relied on the materials from the Belt for the technology and industry, yet they continually oppressed the Belters and refused to allow them to rule themselves. The inyalowda who docked in the Belt were happy to drink Belter liquor, blow off steam in Belter brothels, and buy Belter metal just to sell third-rate materials back. The choicest fruits (and grains, and beef) of Europa and Ganymede went to Mars, and even Earth, before they were shared with the Belt. The corporations most Belters worked for cut corners, resulting in unsafe work conditions for asteroid and water miners. Basic necessities such as water and air were tightly controlled—and shorted during times of financial hardship (for the corporation, that is). Belter habitats were outfitted with recycled and reused air scrubber units, adding to the plague of hypoxia among Belters.

The Butcher of Anderson Station

An example of Inner relations with the Belters and a rallying cry for the Belt was Anderson Station, a resupply center for the Anderson-Hyosung Cooperative Industries Group orbiting at the opposite side of the Belt from Ceres. When the Earth-Mars Coalition administrator implemented a surcharge on already-scarce supply transfers, a Belter insurgency took control of the station. Although they surrendered, a UN Navy task-force led by Colonel Fred Johnson was ordered to retake the station, and did so by force, killing thousands in the process. Surveillance cameras broadcast three days of slaughter across the System. The UN awarded Fred Johnson the Medal of Honor for his actions, but in the Belt, he became infamous as “The Butcher of Anderson Station”. Johnson resigned his commission and publicly apologized for the tragedy. Eventually, he became administrator of Tycho Station and allied himself with the Outer Planets Alliance, seeking justice and representation for all Belters.

The Opa

The Outer Planets Alliance (OPA) looked to change things, to give Belters solidarity and collective strength. Belters showed their support and membership with tattoos like a broken circle around the neck, symbolizing both solidarity and the contact burns and scars the first generations of Belters received from faulty vac-suits. Even more common is the split circle, like a ringed planet seen from the side, which represents the divisions of inner and outer in the System. Still, for all of its talk of unity, the OPA was never really unified, but rather an umbrella term for a collection of inde - pendent cells ostensibly seeking to form an independent Belter nation. Some were nothing more than terrorist cells or criminal gangs, seeking and dealing out violence, killing Inners in the name of Belter unity. Other cells worked with student groups, or sought to foster goodwill, attempting to work towards Belter independence through diplomacy. Still others, such as the Belters aboard Tycho Station, looked to consolidate the wealth of the Belt and use it for political leverage at the bargaining table. While the OPA accomplished some good, it also offered the opportunity for exploitation by Winston Duarte: He supplied the most violent factions of the OPA with ships and weapons and used them as a distraction for his First Fleet to leave the system and transit through the slow zone to Laconia. That “distraction” resulted in the deaths of billions during the Free Navy Conflict and nearly spelled the end of Belters as a people. Horrified by the war-crimes of Belters like Marco Inaros, some Belters sided with the Earth-Mars Coalition, and their courage laid the foundation for the future of the Belt.

Belter Creole

Humanity’s expansion into the system lead to the co-mingling of people from many different regions of Earth or Mars who often didn’t speak the same language. They developed a pidgin creole, lang Belta, to communicate. Lang Belta is interspersed with grammar and vocabulary from Russian, Esperanto, Korean, Chinese, Portuguese, Spanish, French, Dutch, German, Italian, Hungarian, Turkish, and Arabic. When playing or interacting with beltalowda characters in The Expanse RPG, don’t try to construct more than simple phrases, sabe? It gets painful aŭdi and makes the game kaka, coyo. After the first sentence or two in-game, call for a Communication (Expression) roll kennst lang Belta if the character is inyalowda and unfamiliar with Belters. Otherwise pepper the dialogue with few choice phrases from the list below and assume the fluent characters speak tényleges lang Belta too thick to understand and you’re gútegow. The trick, like lang Belta itself, is to ensure everyone gets the gist of the communication, bist bien? Most educated Belters actually speak several languages but won’t do so around inyalowda, otherwise relishing the confusion of Tumang et Pomang.

After the Free Navy Conflict, Earth and Mars were devastated: Earth by asteroid bombardment and Mars by massive civil unrest and the loss of a full third of their military personnel and resources, bleeding away more each day through the Ring and out to other systems. The political leaders of the System saw the Belt as humanity’s salvation and hammered out an agreement to create the Transport Union, an organization to oversee and manage traffic and commerce off-world. Although Chrisjen Avasarala tried to recruit Captain James Holden as the Union’s first President, he instead proposed a Belter, Michio Pa, whose defection from the Free Navy helped turn the tide of the conflict, making her a war hero. The Transport Union gave the Belters true solidarity and political and economic power. What’s more, it gave them a purpose in a universe where humanity was rapidly spreading out among the stars to dive down the gravity wells of more than a thousand terrestrial planets, most of which the Belters could not call home. Their home would remain the expanse between those planets, which makes them uniquely suited to help manage travel through it.

The Union was given authority over the trade routes and traffic, not only through the System, but all of the systems reached by the Ring gates. Planets would continue to govern their own affairs, but the shipment of goods, colonists, and supplies between them would be the purview of the Union. Finally able to share in not only the wealth of the Belt and Outer Planets, but also of numerous colony worlds, the Transport Union quickly became an economic powerhouse able to distribute wealth to its primarily Belter workforce.

Every Belter asteroid, habitat, or structure is purpose-built for human habitation. Nothing natural survives in space. Natural lighting is rare, since the Belt is too far from the Sun. Ultraviolet and full-spectrum lamps flicker in cramped, rock-hewn hallways with moisture collecting on the walls. Most of those walls are meters thick, keeping Belters safe from the radiation pervading the Belt. Even the rare greenhouses have massive lamps or rely on orbiting solar mirrors to gather light and beam it down into them. “The inner planets look on us as their labor force. They tax us. They direct what CERES we do. They enforce their laws and ignore ours in the name of stability. Eight hundred to a thousand ships are docked at Ceres every day, swarmed by Belter dockhands and watched by a million eyes. Transport Union wealth has improved conditions on Ceres to something akin to those found on colonies like Luna or Mars, but life inside a cold rock in space can only get so comfortable. Still, Ceres Station has better maintenance and living conditions than ever before. The top levels of Ceres are a long corridor wrapping around the outer edge of the station, topped by a dome showing an approximation of the sky meant to comfort visitors and residents alike. The gravity lessens the deeper one goes into the station, and a pronounced Coriolis effect pres-Threat: Moderate ents itself: poured liquids curve in the air, while people stumble and suffer from dizziness, nausea, and seasickness millions of miles from the nearest sea. Water on the station is rationed, recycled, and carefully monitored and water-theft remains a criminal racket here as on many stations. The black and grey markets still thrive on Ceres, reinforced with dozens of ships crisscrossing the Belt—and virtually any Belter on board a ship might be tasked with helping out their fellows. Carved crevices and repurposed cargo containers play host all manner of humanity, from miners to prostitutes to mechanics.

The Tycho-Pallas Complex

The Belt headquarters of the Tycho Manufacturing and Engineering Concern, Tycho Station is one of the largest mobile construction platforms in the Sol System. To this day, fifteen thousand workers and their families live within Tycho, building megastructures or massive ships far beyond the reach of a gravity well. A ring station built around a sphere half a kilometer across with more than sixty-five million cubic meters of manufacturing and storage space, Tycho Station boasts two counter-rotating habitation rings, providing the same standard spin-gravity as the rest of the Belt. The top of the manufacturing sphere features massive construction waldos capable of grasping a heavy freighter or securing singularly large ships, such as Medina Station, itself built at Tycho as the generation ship Nauvoo. A capital-ship-class fusion reactor and drive system projecting out of an elongated drive cone makes Tycho capable of relocating itself around the Belt for differing work needs and locales. Each compartment within the titanic rings was built on a swivel system, allowing the chambers to reorient to thrust gravity when needed. Following the formation of the Transport Union, Tycho Station was moved and docked with the asteroid Pallas to form the Tycho- Pallas Complex. Although the venerable Tycho Station is showing its age compared to the newer Void Cities it helped to construct, the station has an important place in Belter history and culture, and the Transport Union means to keep Tycho Station running—and busy building—for as long as they can. Pallas got its start as a refinery, the first in the Belt, but now much of its refined material doesn’t have to go any further than Tycho’s shipyard. Unlike Ceres, Pallas wasn’t spun to generate gravity, so some of the Belters who lived and worked here had some of the most extreme microgravity adaptations and issues. This made Pallas a hotbed for OPA radicalism in the pre-Union era. The Union’s choice of Pallas as a permanent home for Tycho Station was based as much on honoring a center for their partisans as it was on the practicalities of repurposing Pallas’ refining and manufacturing facilities to support Tycho’s manufacturing.

The Void Cities

Since the creation of the Tycho-Pallas Complex, one of the Transport Union’s most ambitious projects has been the construction of the largest vessels ever built by humanity, what the Belters call “void cities.” Built on a superstructure of carbon-silicate ribs based on protomolecule materials science, each void city is a massive rotating drum around a core with 70 decks. An Epstein drive is at one end of the vessel, with docking ports at the other. All of the spaces of the drum are designed to rotate, based on whether the vessel is under thrust or at station-keeping with the drum spinning. The spin is usually kept to only about 0.1 outward g to accommodate the residents, who are nearly all Belters. Each void city has a population of some 200,000, with the greenhouses, gardens, medical facilities, civil spaces, and even nurseries, schools, and childcare necessary to make them true “cities in space.” They also have the weapons systems to make them battleships capable of facing-down anything known among the Inner Planets or from the other side of the ring gates, if necessary. The cities are mobile space stations even more ambitious than Medina, able to serve as mobile resupply, relief, and colonization ports of call in the System. The first of the void cities, Independence, was completed a few years after the Transport Union was formed. It was followed by Guard of Passage and then People’s Home in the following years. Some thirty years after the formation of the Union, a fourth void city, Assurance of Peace, is under construction at Tycho-Pallas.

Transfer Stations

The Transport Union’s next ambitious project after the first void cities was the construction of orbital transfer stations meant to serve as the “gateways” between planets and the space controlled and overseen by the Union. The first, Transfer Station L-5 (TSL-5) will be placed at the Lagrange-5 point trailing the orbit of Luna, meant to serve the Earth-Luna system and to free the Transport Union from the need to rely on facilities on Luna or ships in orbit. The station’s habitation ring is some 2100 meters in diameter and can hold more than 20,000 people. Its domed central section has berths for hundreds of ships and storage space for the transfer of vast amounts of cargo, making it a waystation for ships to load and offload cargo for transfer by shuttle to the planet below. Once TSL-5 is complete, the Transport Union has plans to construct similar transfer stations in orbit of all inhabited planets that it services, further facilitating and expanding shipping and travel.

Like how the gold rush sent Americans across a continent and into the wilderness to seek their fortune, once the stars were in reach, humanity spread across the Belt and beyond for similar reasons. The hundreds of small settlements, stations, and ships that form the Belt were built around the same time as the shipyards, stations, mines, and settlements of the Outer Planets. Although Belters are considered the heart and soul of the OPA, it was named the Outer Planets Alliance for a reason. The major moons of Jupiter and Saturn have fully-functioning settlements buried within. Indeed, the Jovian and Saturnian Systems are so large and well-populated they could be almost be considered tiny solar systems of their own. The Uranian and Neptunian Systems are far more sparsely populated and were often ignored by the Inners unless it was time to collect tariffs or taxes. Though not actually within the Belt, these systems were settled by Belters—and their inhabitants have a shared history and culture. Now the Outer Planets are very much the domain of the Transport Union, the gateway to Sol, with the literal passage of the ring gate at their outer boundary.

text.content:
JUPITER

The Jovian System has the largest population in the Outer Planets, who have made a home on Jupiter’s moons. The planet itself is uninhabitable, but there are dozens of settlements and orbiting stations around it and its moons. Metis, Adrastea, Amalthea, and Thebe are unpopulated primarily due to their proximity to Jupiter’s radiation belts. Even the aboveground structures on moons further from the planet require heavy shielding. Leda, Himalia, Lysithea, Elara, Ananke, Carme, Pasiphae, and Sinope are all too small to support colonies or activities beyond some mining and resource harvesting. The Jovian System is responsible for growing and distributing most of the food in the Outers and the Belt. Most extrasolar astronomy was done in the Jovian System before the Uranian System was colonized. It is a vital piece of humanity’s survival in the furthest reaches of the solar system, and of the Belt’s economy.

Callisto

This large moon’s tectonic stability and significant deposits of rare minerals made it an ideal location for shipyards, and for a time Earth and Mars both had ship-building facilities on Callisto. This lead to occasional tensions, including the so-called Callisto Insurrection, a proxy war between Earth and Mars involving Belter groups fighting each other rather than their Inner Planets “advisors.” Prior to the Free Navy Conflict, a Free Navy commando team attacked the Martian shipyards, stealing Martian stealth-technology to use in the asteroid bombardment of Earth. They covered up the theft with a massive kinetic strike on the site that destroyed it, resulting in secondary damage to the colony’s infrastructure, including cracking and depressurizing at least one of its hard shelters. During the Free Navy Conflict itself, Callisto allied itself with the Free Navy and eventually became its de facto command center after Marco Inaros abandoned Ceres. After the Conflict, the Transport Union diverted funds to help shore up the Callisto colony and mining operations, although the shipyards remain a mere shadow of their former selves. Shipbuilding has shifted elsewhere in the System, but there’s still a need for the materials Callisto can provide, as well as small-scale ship construction, repair, and maintenance. Port Hampton is the moon’s only settlement, dug into the walls of a large crater used as a launching point for ships carrying mineral cargos. Like many cities built around industries requiring hard physical labor and long work hours, it has a frontier town reputation: a place to party and blow off steam during off-hours. Most of its permanent inhabitants are involved in businesses that profit from those off-hours. A private Transport Union hired security force handles any issues that stem from disorderly conduct.

Io

Io, one of Jupiter’s larger moons, has an atmosphere of sulfur dioxide and hotspots of volcanic and tectonic activity, making it an extremely hostile and unforgiving environment. So what makes people consider living there? Money, of course. In addition to Io’s volcanos producing vents of intense heat, the moon itself creates an intense electrical field when its nickel-iron core passes through Jupiter’s magnetic field, producing in excess of 1 trillion watts. SATURNsettlements or facilities of one type or another. Saturn’s infamous “lost” moon, Phoebe—which was not a moon at all—was also the catalyst that changed the course of humanity forever.

Phoebe

In the early days of Phoebe’s colonization, the story was that Mars established a science station and later collaborated with the Protogen corporation to study early solar system formation and Oort cloud objects. Study of the moon suggested, from its unique, eccentric, retrograde orbit and unusual albedo, that it might have been a captured comet or Kuiper Belt object. Phoebe proved unique in other ways. Scientists discovered unusual silicate structures within the moon, which turned out to be a kind of molecular-level biotechnology of clearly alien origin. They theorized that, rather than being from the Kuiper Belt, Phoebe was an extrasolar object, possibly aimed directly at the Sol system. Any remnants, caught in Saturn’s — Leviathan Wakes gravity, fell into its atmosphere or possibly scattered into its rings.

Titan

The most populous moon in the Saturnian system has a thick cloud cover that generates strange and beautiful solar wind displays as the moon moves in and out of Saturn’s powerful magnetic field. These stunning storms and formations are visible from the aboveground domed habitats on Titan, providing the moon’s main source of income: tourism. The moon is a popular vacation spot for visitors from the Outers, and sometimes even those from the Inner Planets will make the long journey to spend a few weeks on Titan, watching the spectacle of colorful clouds and eating in the best restaurants the Outer Planets have to offer. Those with means may sojourn in the moon’s exclusive and famous pleasure domes. Due to both food production and tourist cash, Titan’s economy is strong. If someone on the moon isn’t working, it’s because they don’t want to, or are unable.

Aside from Earth, Titan is also the most chemically active body in the solar system. Both its atmosphere and icy surface are filled with organic compounds not found anywhere else. Easy access to ice suitable for oxygen and water production and a lack of available sunlight have put Titan on the forefront of sunlight-free food production. The yeasts, fungi, and other compounds produced as food TITAN on the moon might be considered strange to those accustomed to food grown in the dirt, but Titan is a long, long way from Earth. Titan fell into the sphere of the Free Navy, and one of the major offensives of the Conflict was fought above the moon, with high casualties on both sides. Survivors were treated to recovery in some of Titan’s hotels and spas, which had been converted into field hospitals. The moon has since resumed its previous economic activities, although now many of the visitors to Titan are newly well-to-do Belters enjoying its amenities and light gravity while appreciating the unique show offered by its colorful atmosphere. Still, a trip to Titan remains only within the means of the wealthy, even in the Transport Union’s time.

Rhea

One of the frontiers of human civilization, Rhea is primarily composed of water, ice, and rock. The only thing the moon has to offer the rest of the System is helium-3 deposits and some small mineral mining operations. Rhea’s several underground habitats provide all the living space required

Iapetus

Since the destruction of Pheobe, Iapetus is the only one of Saturn’s moons that does not orbit within range of the equator. Aside from that, the moon is primarily known for its leading and trailing hemispheres being radically different. The albedo of most of the leading hemisphere is as dark as lampblack, while the trailing hemisphere’s albedo as bright as Europa. The most recent prevailing theory for the odd phenomenon is Iapetus must have absorbed another, darker body at some point in its history. Whatever it was, and whatever the cause, the leading side of Iapetus is covered in minerals ready for harvesting. Colonists have built special mechs that make regular runs to sweep the surface for these materials for export and sale. Because this type of surface mining costs so much less than traditional methods the moon has been able to support itself entirely through mineral sweeping. Discovery of helium-3 deposits and the building of refineries has only strengthened and diversified the economy. Most of Iapetus’ residents work in the collection and refinement of minerals for export and live in its small group of underground habitats. The notion Iapetus might have some connection with extrasolar objects has also drawn some attention and scientific research, with authorities in the system keeping a close eye on the results, just in case any evidence of yet another alien object should turn up.

URANUSThe Uranian system is best known for extrasolar astronomy, peering outwards from the dim light of Sol to the distant stars, and for the (relatively) nearby presence of the Sol ring, just about two AU further out. This, and the Neptunian system, are the edge of human civilization, where only the fearless and the desperate venture—for better or worse.

Titania

The first and only of Uranus’ moons to be settled by colonists, this “ice ball” orbiting Uranus is so far from the sun that almost no solar energy can be captured. Materials must be imported from other systems to generate fusion energy, though there is hope the necessary materials can be found in the other surrounding moons. Ice is the one thing that is plentiful, so water and oxygen are not an issue, but organic material is practically nonexistent and must be imported as well. The few thousand people living on the moon are pioneers, and their existence is accordingly stark.

The Ring

The key thing that changed life on Titania was the Ring. Its proximity to Uranus’ orbit makes Titania one of the closest human outposts to the mysterious artifact. Of course, the planet’s orbit is vast, and the ring isn’t leashed to Uranus, so that usefulness is diminishing as the distance between the planetary system and the ring slowly widens. Still, for now, the Titanians are both grateful for the added resources to their colony and slightly resentful of outsiders who merely find them a convenient stopover. The Sol ring, and its network, are detailed in Chapter 11.

pages.name: The Outer Planets: The Neptunian System

text.content:
The most distant of the planets, the ice giant Neptune is dark, cold, and constantly under the force of supersonic windstorms. Its moons are not much better; so far from the sun it is little more than a bright star in the sky. They are largely considered uninhabitable at this time, but so were the moons of Uranus, once upon a time. That said, the opening of the Sol ring means most of humanity’s attention stops at the orbit of Uranus, and Neptune is largely considered too far out, with too little to offer, for anyone to bother with it—a notion the Transport Union has followed in the years since its formation.

Triton

Of Neptune’s moons, Triton is the largest, and the only moon in the solar system with a retrograde orbit. Due to this orbit and a composition comparable to Pluto’s, scientists believe that the moon may have been a dwarf planet from the Kuiper Belt captured in Neptune’s orbit. The mass of ice on its surface and below ground can produce both water and oxygen. Tectonic activity, complete with nitrogen gas geysers, makes work directly on the surface perilous, but underground habitats in stable tectonic areas are thought to be reasonably safe. Only a hardy and motley band of astronomers and prospectors live on Triton. The deep astronomy labs are responsible for charting into the unexplored reaches of the galaxy, while prospectors explore the mining possibilities on Neptune’s moons. Astronomical research on Neptune currently devotes considerable time to using parallax mapping to try and pinpoint the locations of systems beyond the ring gates, figuring out where they are in proximity to Earth, or even if they are all in the Milky Way Galaxy at all. Briefly, after the destruction of the Canterbury inflamed the System, prospectors sympathetic to the OPA seized control of the astronomy labs on Triton. They turned the imaging array in-system and broadcast the location of every Martian ship they observed—even though the “coup” was short-lived.
